feedback: If the chain is scrambled, return to a single fully worked example and rebuild it before attempting a new system.
If a learner treats systems as isolated, prompt: 'Where does the oxygen the circulatory system carries actually come from?' to surface the respiratory–circulatory link.
If a learner names an interaction but gives no exchanged material, ask what is being passed between the two systems (e.g. oxygen, nutrients).
activities.intendedInsight: Building and sequencing the levels makes the learner actively construct the hierarchy; connecting two systems moves them from labelling to systems reasoning — the body functions because subsystems interact, not in isolation.
learnerActions: Arrange cards (muscle cell, muscle tissue, heart, circulatory system, human) into the correct nested order, from smallest building block to whole organism.

When an order is correct, assemble a second worked chain for a different system to show the pattern repeats — for example a digestive chain: gland/epithelial cell → epithelial tissue → stomach → digestive system → human (one illustrative strand; real organs contain several tissue types).
Pick two organ systems and explain how they interact — for example, the respiratory system supplies oxygen that the circulatory system distributes around the body.
Write or say a short argument, supported by this example, for why the body works as a system of interacting subsystems.
activities.title: Build the body and connect two systems

feedback: Correct order: cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism. If a learner recites this but cannot explain how a tissue is made of cells or why a heart is an organ rather than a tissue, that signals recall without understanding — return to the worked chain and the 'built-from-many' relation.
Watch for muddling 'organ' with 'organism': distinguish an organ (the heart) from the whole organism (the animal).
If a learner thinks any group of cells is a tissue, stress the 'similar/specialised cells working together on one job' definition.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to place any part, name its neighbours, and explain 'built from many of the level below' distinguishes genuine understanding from memorised word order.
learnerActions: Order the five levels from smallest building block up to the whole organism: cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism.
For a given example, match it to its level (e.g. 'cardiac muscle' → tissue; 'heart' → organ).
Answer: 'A group of similar cells working together is a…?' and justify the answer.

For a given example structure (e.g. a muscle cell, cardiac muscle, the stomach, the digestive system), state its level and name the level directly above and directly below it where one exists (a cell has no level below it in this hierarchy).
Explain in a sentence how each level above the cell is made from several or many units of the level before it (not just recite the order).
activities.title: Place any body part and explain how levels are built
